Inside the Cache: From Silicon to Embedded ML

The Memory Wall

Why caches exist — and why, even now, they are the quiet reason your code either flies or crawls.

Your CPU is mostly waiting

There's a slightly embarrassing fact about the computer you're reading this on. Most of the time, its CPU isn't computing. It's waiting. Waiting for a number to arrive from memory so it can do something with it. A chip advertised as "4 GHz" finishes a clock tick every quarter of a nanosecond, but the DRAM it talks to takes somewhere between 60 and 100 nanoseconds to hand over a single value. In CPU time, that's a few hundred ticks of doing absolutely nothing. If you ran your processor without any tricks at all, it would spend more of its life idle than a bored teenager on a Sunday afternoon.

This gap between how fast a processor can work and how fast memory can feed it has a name. Engineers started calling it the memory wall in the mid-1990s, when it became obvious that CPU speeds were climbing roughly 50% per year while DRAM latency was inching down at maybe 7%. The two lines on the graph were pulling apart fast, and nobody had a way to close them back together. Three decades later, the wall hasn't come down. It's been papered over. And the wallpaper is the entire reason this series exists.

The processor is fast. Memory is slow. Everything clever in modern hardware is a response to that one stubborn fact.

What "fast" and "slow" actually feel like

Latency numbers in nanoseconds are technically precise and emotionally useless. Your brain wasn't built to feel the difference between 1 ns and 100 ns. So people who work on this stuff for a living tend to rescale the numbers into something humans can picture. If one CPU cycle were one second long, how long would each layer of memory take?

That scaling turns the memory wall from a graph into something you can see in your head. A register access is a second. An L1 cache hit is three or four seconds. An L2 hit is about ten. L3 is roughly a minute. And a trip to main memory? Closer to five or six minutes. Going to an SSD is a week. A network round trip is a year. Try it in the toggle below.

How far away is "memory", really?

Toggle between real nanoseconds and human-scale time. In nanoseconds the bars all look manageable, almost comparable. Flip to human scale and the registers/L1 become a breath while main memory becomes a lunch break. That's the wall. Every trick in the rest of this series is a way to avoid the long bars and keep the work happening in the short ones.

Why not just make DRAM faster?

The natural reaction, the first time you see these numbers, is to ask why we don't just build faster DRAM and be done with it. It's a reasonable question, and the answer is physics and economics in roughly equal parts.

DRAM stores each bit as a tiny bit of charge on a capacitor. Capacitors leak. So every few milliseconds the chip has to stop what it's doing, read every cell, and write it back to keep the charge alive. This is where the "dynamic" in Dynamic RAM comes from, and it's also why DRAM is physically different from the SRAM that lives inside your CPU. SRAM keeps each bit as the stable state of a little six-transistor circuit. No leak, no refresh, and much faster. The catch: SRAM uses roughly six transistors per bit while DRAM uses one transistor plus one capacitor. Same bit, six times the silicon area. Build a 16 GB memory out of SRAM and the price tag goes from "a few hundred dollars" to "a small house."

We can have memory that is fast, large, or cheap. Pick two. Any two.

So the industry made peace with a compromise that everyone hates and nobody can improve on. Keep a small amount of truly fast memory close to the CPU. Keep a large amount of slow memory far from the CPU. Then spend enormous amounts of engineering effort making sure the data you're about to need is, somehow, already in the fast part.

The hierarchy

That compromise is what the memory hierarchy is. Not a design, really. More like a truce. Each layer trades size for speed, sitting between your CPU and the sluggish main memory.

At the top, registers. A handful of them per core, single-cycle access, invisible to the compiler most of the time. Below that, L1 cache, usually split into two halves: one for instructions (the code your CPU is running) and one for data (the values it's chewing on). L1 is tiny by modern standards, typically 32 to 64 KB per core, but it responds in about four cycles. Below that, L2, a few hundred kilobytes to a megabyte, around a dozen cycles. Below that, L3, shared between all cores on the chip, tens of megabytes, forty or fifty cycles to answer. And only after all of those misses does the request finally trudge off to DRAM, where the wait begins.

You'll see that first level called "L1I" and "L1D" in datasheets and performance counters. The split is deliberate. Instructions and data have very different access patterns, and pretending they don't would cost you throughput. That's the first hint, buried right in the architecture, that caches aren't just "small fast storage." They're shaped by the workloads that use them. We'll come back to that idea more than once.

Each level is a smaller, faster bet that you'll want the same data again soon.

Why the bet usually pays off

It would be astonishing if a cache worked at all. You'd need the processor to ask for the same small set of values, over and over, while it has a whole multi-gigabyte address space to roam around in. And yet the bet wins almost every time, because real programs are not random. They have two very strong habits.

The first is called temporal locality. If you touched a memory address a moment ago, you'll probably touch it again soon. Think about how often a loop variable gets read and written. Think about how many times the top of the stack is used in a given second. Variables are re-used, not visited once and abandoned.

The second is spatial locality. If you touched an address, you're probably about to touch the one right next to it. Walking through an array is the obvious case, but it's everywhere. Fields in a struct sit next to each other. Instructions execute in sequence most of the time. Even a jump usually lands in code that was already sitting nearby.

Caches turn both of these habits into a free lunch. Temporal locality means keeping a recently-used value around is worth it. Spatial locality means fetching a value's neighbours while you're at it costs almost nothing extra and usually pays off. This is why caches fetch data in chunks called cache lines, typically 64 bytes at a time, instead of the single bytes you might have expected. You ask for one number. The hardware quietly brings back sixteen. Eight of them, you'll want. That's the deal.

Both patterns visit every cell exactly once. The sequential walk rides spatial locality — one miss pulls in a whole line of neighbours and everything after is free. The random walk gets nothing for free. Hit Run and watch the right panel bleed red.

A cache line here is 4 cells wide. On a sequential walk, the first visit to a line misses and fetches all four cells together — the next three visits in that line are hits, for free. On the random walk, the probability that your next jump lands inside a line you just fetched is tiny, so almost every access pays the full miss cost. Same amount of work. Radically different time.

What this means for the code you actually write

If you've ever wondered why a transposed matrix multiply can be ten times slower than a normal one, or why iterating a 2D array in the "wrong" order tanks your benchmarks, you've already run head-first into the memory wall without knowing its name. The loops were identical. The arithmetic was identical. The only thing that changed was the order you touched memory in, and with it whether each access was a hit (fast) or a miss (slow). A dozen-line change in a loop can move you from 95% hit rate to 50% hit rate, and that cliff is often the entire difference between "production-ready" and "unusable."

Your code isn't slow because the CPU is slow. It's slow because the cache doesn't have what the CPU asked for.

This is especially sharp on embedded targets, where L2 might be a few hundred kilobytes and L3 doesn't even exist. Push a neural network through a Cortex-M with the wrong weight layout and you'll watch inference time triple while power consumption climbs. The arithmetic didn't get harder. The data just stopped arriving on time. We'll spend a lot of the later posts on exactly that class of problem.

Where this is going

This post named the enemy. The rest of the series is about the machinery we use to hold it back.

The next post cracks open a cache line and shows you what a lookup actually looks like, bit by bit: tag, index, offset, and why your address gets sliced up the particular way it does. After that, we'll look at the organizational choices (direct-mapped, set-associative, fully associative) and the pathology each one creates. Then replacement policies, miss taxonomies, write behaviours, coherence between cores, DMA, the TLB. Every post is another lever the hardware gives you to fight the wall.

By the end of the series, we'll use all of those levers together to make a small neural network run efficiently on embedded hardware — the kind of target where you can't just throw another gigabyte of RAM at the problem and hope. The memory wall is the villain. Caches are the response. And the response has a lot more structure than it looks like from the outside.

Caches exist because memory is too slow. Everything that follows is about teaching caches to guess well.
